uncited: This family encompasses the low-level algorithms and hardware mechanisms used to execute volume rendering computations on parallel architectures, primarily GPUs and multi-core CPUs.
It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential ray casting and compositing by distributing work across thousands of threads.

What sets this family apart from sibling methods like [Ray-primitive intersection](769-ray-primitive-intersection.md) and [Ray generation and camera models](770-ray-generation-and-camera-models.md) is its focus on the execution model, memory synchronization, and data parallelism infrastructure rather than the geometric or optical mathematics of the ray itself.
The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores).
Push width and height as `uint32_t[2]` constants.
Transition swapchain image layout from `eUndefined` to `eGeneral`.
Transition image layout to `eColorAttachmentOptimal` if GUI is enabled, else `ePresentSrcKHR`.
Calculate the dot product of arbitrary sized vectors using the `cublasSDot` function with necessary parameters.
Point-wise multiplication is performed in the kernel, storing results in shared memory sized to the number of threads in the block.
Assign tasks associated with each subvolume to processors.
Parallel render each subvolume to generate p distributed subimages.
Parallel and GPU primitives have evolved alongside the development of General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU).
Early volume rendering relied on CPU-based ray casting, which was computationally prohibitive for high-resolution volumes.
